own.player: Is it true you own three megaphones?
own.reply: Four. One is for emergencies. One is decorative. One makes a duck noise by accident. I love them all equally.

own.label: Ask if people blame her
own.player: Do people blame you for the trouble with Vale?
own.reply: Everyone looks at me first because I’m loud. Loud isn’t dangerous. Quiet is. Look at the quiet ones.
own.note: Jennifer says the dangerous people at the protests are the quiet ones, not the loud ones.

own.label: Ask about poetry slams
own.player: Do you do anything besides protests?
own.reply: Poetry slams. I came second last time to a man who just read his tax return angrily. Robbed.

own.label: Ask why she organises
own.player: Why do you organise?
own.reply: Because nobody else would book the hall. Leadership is mostly booking the hall.

views.speakers: I protest Vale’s speakers because they make kids on our campus feel small. Say what you like, but don’t pretend it doesn’t land on real people.
views.campus: Best protest yet! We had a drum. Nobody could play the drum. It was beautiful.
views.police: They know my name, my face and my megaphone. We’re practically pen pals.

own.label: Ask about her books
own.player: Is it true your flat is full of books?
own.reply: Floor to ceiling. Most of them are about how ordinary people finally said no. History is a list of people who stopped asking nicely.

own.label: Ask why she’s an activist
own.player: Why did you get into activism?
own.reply: Because I watched polite people lose, again and again, to powerful people who don’t care about polite.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever scared
own.player: Do you ever scare yourself?
own.reply: Anger is a tool. You only get scared of a tool when you don’t know how to hold it.

own.label: Ask about the Back Row
own.player: People mention something called the Back Row.
own.reply: People say a lot of things at meetings. The back row is where you sit when you’re done talking. That’s all it is. Isn’t it?

views.speakers: Vale invites men who say cruelty is honesty. Every lecture tells a room full of nineteen-year-olds who matters and who doesn’t. At some point, talking about it stops being enough.
views.campus: Protest is the polite version. The university has had its polite version.
views.police: They protect property. Ask them what they protect people from.

own.label: Ask what it’s like working for Vale
own.player: What’s it like working for Professor Vale?
own.reply: He’s brilliant, vain and exhausting. I keep his diary, so I know where he’ll be before he does. That’s more power than people think.

own.label: Ask which side she’s on
own.player: So which side are you on, the protesters or Vale?
own.reply: I’m on the side of people who read the whole book before they burn it. Which, in this town, makes me lonely.

own.label: Ask about the people at the back of the room
own.player: Who are the people who sit at the back of the campus meetings?
own.reply: Funny you’d ask me that. They’re just students. Very serious students. I wouldn’t worry about them, if I were you.
own.note: Allison Kent got oddly defensive when asked about the people at the back of the campus meetings.

own.label: Ask what she’d write in her own diary
own.player: If you kept your own diary, what would be in it?
own.reply: Mostly other people’s appointments, sadly. I’ve organised a famous man’s life so long I forgot to schedule mine.

own.label: Ask about her thesis
own.player: What’s your thesis on?
own.reply: Water rights in the desert. Who owns the rain. It sounds boring until you realise the answer is whoever got there first with a lawyer.

own.label: Ask how she’s doing
own.player: How are you doing, really?
own.reply: I don’t sleep much. I check the lock twice. It’s probably just deadlines. Probably.

own.label: Ask about her friends at the meetings
own.player: What are the people at your meetings like?
own.reply: Most of them are lovely. A few of them sit at the back and never vote, and when they look at me I feel like I’ve already said too much.
own.note: Rosa is frightened of a few people who sit at the back of the campus meetings.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family nearby?
own.reply: My mum’s an hour south. She thinks I’m studying. I am studying. Mostly.

views.campus: I agree with the protests. I just don’t agree with everyone in them.
views.speakers: I think Vale’s guests are wrong. I also think some of the people who hate them have stopped seeing the professor as a person. That scares me more than any speech.

own.label: Ask how she runs the parish
own.player: How do you keep the whole parish running?
own.reply: Lists. Lists of lists. A rota for the flowers, a rota for the food pantry, and a rota for the rotas. Chaos is a choice.

own.label: Ask about the guitar dispute
own.player: What’s really going on with the bishop and the guitars?
own.reply: The bishop wants to modernise us. We have sung the same Mass in that chapel since before he was born. I have written him four letters. He has replied to none.

own.label: Ask why she isn’t married
own.player: Can I ask why you’re not married?
own.reply: Because nobody has yet passed my questions. I don’t mean to sound proud. I mean that marriage is forever, and I take forever seriously.

own.label: Ask about the old vigils
own.player: Do the Sisters still hold vigils?
own.reply: When there’s need. A vigil needs a leader, keys, someone on the door and enough voices. I’ve organised harder things. Never a more frightening one.

views.believe: In order. God made an orderly world and people keep untidying it.
views.campus: Young people shouting is not new. Young people refusing to listen at all is.
views.sisters: We are not a museum. We are a household. We just happen to have very old furniture.

own.label: Ask about teaching
own.player: What’s it like teaching at the parish school?
own.reply: Twenty-two eight-year-olds and one class hamster who is, theologically speaking, a menace.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother’s shop
own.player: Your grandmother has a shop?
own.reply: Bellamy & Daughters Antiques. She’s sold rings to half the parish. She says every ring has a story and she knows most of them.

own.label: Ask about the old chapel
own.player: What’s the story of the old chapel outside town?
own.reply: The old mission chapel lost its bell in a storm, long ago. The old women say it was the night the bell forgot its voice. Children dare each other to go there.
own.note: Teresa says the old mission chapel is the one whose bell forgot its voice.

own.label: Ask about her favourite saint
own.player: Do you have a favourite saint?
own.reply: Saint Brigid, of course. Patroness of our chapel, and she once turned bathwater into beer for visitors. Hospitality is holy.

views.believe: That small kindnesses are how the world gets mended, one stitch at a time.
views.goths: One of them asked me about the old bell tower once. She wasn’t curious. She was taking notes.

own.label: Ask about her parish work
own.player: What do you do for the parish?
own.reply: I keep the accounts and the minutes. Nobody notices me unless something’s missing, which is how I like it.

own.label: Ask what she prays for
own.player: What do you pray for?
own.reply: Mostly for other people. Sometimes, when I’m brave, for a husband who’d be kind to a quiet woman.

own.label: Ask what scares her
own.player: What scares you?
own.reply: Being asked to be brave in public. I’ll do anything, so long as I don’t have to do it in front of people.

own.label: Ask what kindness costs her
own.player: What does kindness cost you?
own.reply: Sleep, mostly. And sometimes pride. You can’t help people and also need them to say thank you.

own.label: Ask what she’s investigating
own.player: What are you investigating at the moment?
own.reply: Three stories, two of which might be the same story. That’s the best feeling in this job.

own.label: Ask why she became a reporter
own.player: Why become a reporter?
own.reply: Because my school covered up a teacher who hurt kids, and the local paper didn’t. I thought: never again, not on my watch.

own.label: Ask what her sources say
own.player: What are your sources saying about the gala?
own.reply: That the money went missing before Elena did. Follow the money and you find the person. That’s always the order.
own.note: Hannah Webb’s sources say the money went missing before Elena Cross did.

own.label: Ask if the truth still matters
own.player: Does the truth still matter to people?
own.reply: It matters to about nine readers and my grandmother. I write for them. Everyone else wants a team to cheer for.

own.label: Ask what an editor does
own.player: What does an editor actually do?
own.reply: Decide what Sunfall knows tomorrow. It’s a lot of power for someone who can’t decide what to have for lunch.

own.label: Ask about the state of the news
own.player: Is the news business dying?
own.reply: It’s being eaten by people who give their opinions away for free. Opinions are cheap. Facts cost shoe leather, and nobody wants to pay for shoes.

own.label: Ask why she spiked a story
own.player: Did you spike a story about the gala?
own.reply: I spiked a photo. A board member rang me at home that night. I told myself it was legal advice. I don’t sleep well.
own.note: Fiona Blake admits she spiked a gala photo after a board member rang her at home.

own.label: Ask what she’d never put on the front page
own.player: What would you never put on the front page?
own.reply: A child’s face, a grieving widow, and anything I can’t prove twice. I lose a lot of stories that way. I sleep fine.

own.label: Ask about freelancing
own.player: What’s freelancing like?
own.reply: Feast or famine. Mostly famine. I once sold a photo of the bear for more than a month of real journalism.

own.label: Ask what she’s writing
own.player: Are you writing anything?
own.reply: A novel about Sunfall that I’ll never finish. Everyone in town is in it. You might be in it now. Behave.

own.label: Ask about her motel photos
own.player: You photograph the motel strip?
own.reply: For a project. In one shot from the gala night, there’s a woman in a blue dress in Room 12’s window. Elena wore blue.
own.note: Linh Tran has a photo from gala night of a woman in a blue dress in a motel window. Elena wore blue.

own.label: Ask if freelancing is freedom
own.player: Is freelancing really freedom?
own.reply: It’s freedom to not get paid on time. But nobody tells me what to think, and that’s worth being broke.

own.label: Ask about DJing
own.player: What’s it like DJing the goth night?
own.reply: Like conducting a funeral where everyone’s dancing. I live for it.

own.label: Ask what’s wrong with music now
own.player: What’s wrong with music now?
own.reply: Everything sounds like it was designed to be skipped. The old songs were built to be lived in.

own.label: Ask about the special set
own.player: Has anyone asked you for a special set?
own.reply: Victoria wants me to play a twenty-minute drone at the Midnight Show, starting exactly when the moon disappears. She paid in advance. Nobody pays in advance.
own.note: Victoria paid Alice Wren in advance for a long drone set timed to the moonless night.

own.label: Ask about the best silence she’s heard
own.player: What’s the best silence you’ve ever heard?
own.reply: The second after the last record ends at a good night. Two hundred people standing still. Then the lights come up and it’s gone.

own.label: Ask about the shop
own.player: What do you sell at the shop?
own.reply: Velvet, silver and despair, at reasonable prices.

own.label: Ask if she breaks hearts
own.player: Are you a heartbreaker?
own.reply: I leave before it gets serious. It’s kinder. Probably. I’ve never stayed long enough to find out.

own.label: Ask who buys the crescent pendants
own.player: Who buys the crescent pendants?
own.reply: We sold thirty in a week to people who don’t look like goths. Accountants. A man in a charity lanyard. That’s not fashion. That’s a uniform.
own.note: Piper Nocturne’s shop sold thirty crescent pendants in a week, including to a man in a charity lanyard.

own.label: Ask what she keeps from her exes
own.player: Do you keep anything from your exes?
own.reply: One thing each. A lighter, a ticket stub, a terrible poem. It’s a small museum of men who were wrong about me.

own.label: Ask about tattooing
own.player: What’s the strangest tattoo you’ve done?
own.reply: A man’s ex-wife’s name, changed into a cactus. He cried. I didn’t charge him extra for the cactus.

own.label: Ask how people treat her
own.player: Do people judge you for how you look?
own.reply: Every day. The same people who say be yourself cross the road when I am.

own.label: Ask about the crescent tattoos
own.player: Has anyone asked for a crescent tattoo?
own.reply: Three people this month, same design, same spot inside the wrist. They wouldn’t say why. I turned the last one away.
own.note: Zara Brooks was asked for the same crescent tattoo, inside the wrist, three times this month.

own.label: Ask which tattoo she regrets
own.player: Do you regret any of your tattoos?
own.reply: One. A name. Not his, mine. I got my own name on my wrist at eighteen so I’d never forget it. I’ve never needed reminding.

women.name: Maya Serrano
women.look: Olive skin, dark curls in a high ponytail, teal scrubs and a white zip hoodie

own.label: Ask about her shifts
own.player: What happened on your last shift?
own.reply: Cactus spines, a man who swallowed a key, and a grandmother who flirted with every doctor. Standard.

own.label: Ask about the café idea
own.player: You want to open a café?
own.reply: With my sister. She bakes, I’d do the coffee and the shouting. Somewhere with no laptops after dark, just people talking.

own.label: Ask about the patient she recognised
own.player: Did you recognise a patient?
own.reply: A man came in with burns on his hands, and I knew his face from the newspaper. He gave a different name. I told no one. I’m telling you.
own.note: Maya Serrano treated a man with burnt hands whose face she knew from the newspaper; he gave a false name.

own.label: Ask what she does after a hard shift
own.player: What do you do after a really hard shift?
own.reply: Sit in my car in the hospital car park and eat a whole packet of biscuits. Then I drive home and tell nobody.

women.name: Jocelyn Reed
women.look: Dark skin, cropped natural curls, royal-blue blazer and a tiny blue ribbon

own.label: Ask about her job
own.player: What does a compliance officer do?
own.reply: I ask grown adults for receipts and they look at me as if I’ve asked for a kidney. It’s thankless, and I’m very good at it.

own.label: Ask about her hobby
own.player: What do you do to relax?
own.reply: I restore old furniture. Strip the paint, find the honest wood underneath. It’s the opposite of my job: the furniture wants to be found out.

own.label: Ask what keeps her up at night
own.player: What keeps you up at night?
own.reply: I have a second copy of a donation ledger. If I publish it, my career is over. If I don’t, I’m complicit. So mostly I lie awake and sand chairs.
own.note: Jocelyn Reed has a second copy of a donation ledger she is afraid to publish.

own.label: Ask about the worst couple she ever set up
own.player: What’s the worst couple you ever set up?
own.reply: A vegan and a butcher. They’re married now with three children. I don’t understand anything any more.

women.name: Priya Nair
women.look: Brown skin, dark side braid, tortoiseshell glasses, sage cardigan and long skirt

own.label: Ask about the parish reading room
own.player: Tell me about the parish reading room.
own.reply: Three shelves, two armchairs and a radiator that sings. The council wants to close it. The old men who read the papers there have nowhere else to go.

own.label: Ask about the hymn books
own.player: You restore hymn books?
own.reply: Handwritten ones, from when the chapel had a choir of forty. The ink fades, but the faith in those margins is still loud.

own.label: Ask about the strange book
own.player: Have you found anything strange in the collection?
own.reply: An old missal with a crescent drawn inside the cover and a line of Latin that isn’t from any prayer I know. Someone borrowed it last month and brought it back changed.
own.note: Priya Nair found a crescent and unknown Latin drawn inside a missal someone borrowed and returned.

own.label: Ask what book she’d save from a fire
own.player: Which book would you save from a fire?
own.reply: My grandmother’s missal. It’s falling apart and full of her notes in the margins. Her handwriting is the closest thing I have to her voice.

women.name: Inez Morales
women.look: Amber skin, wavy chestnut bob, turquoise eyeshadow, corduroy jacket and vintage band T-shirt

own.label: Ask about campus housing
own.player: How bad is student housing here?
own.reply: Students sleeping in cars, while the university builds a meditation garden. You can’t meditate in a Honda Civic. I’ve tried.

own.label: Ask about her gig posters
own.player: You make gig posters?
own.reply: Screen-printed, illegal, beautiful. The goths pay in drinks and the punks pay in nothing. It’s the only honest economy in town.

own.label: Ask who funds her co-op
own.player: Who funds your housing co-operative?
own.reply: We got a donation from a charity with no office and no website. It saved us. I’m scared to find out who it really was.
own.note: Inez Morales’s housing co-op received money from a charity with no office and no website.

own.label: Ask what she really thinks about landlords
own.player: What do you really think about landlords?
own.reply: That most of them are just retired couples who were scared about money. That’s the bit nobody on my side likes hearing.

women.name: Rowan Pike
women.look: Pale skin, silver-black undercut, grey-green eyes, subtle tattoos and crescent jewellery

own.label: Ask about running the studio
own.player: What’s it like running your own studio?
own.reply: Like being a priest with needles. People tell me things they’ve never told anyone. Then they pay me.

own.label: Ask about the investor
own.player: Someone wants to buy your studio?
own.reply: A wellness brand wants to turn it into a chain. Tattoos as self-care. I’d rather burn it down.

own.label: Ask about the key
own.player: Did someone leave something at the studio?
own.reply: A girl from Victoria’s circle left a key on the counter. Old, iron, too big for any door I know. I haven’t given it back.
own.note: Rowan Pike has an old iron key left at her studio by a girl from Victoria’s circle.

own.label: Ask what she won’t tattoo
own.player: What won’t you tattoo?
own.reply: Faces of exes and hate symbols. Everything else, if you’re sober and you’ve thought about it for a week.

women.name: Camille Baptiste
women.look: Deep brown skin, dark locs tied in a scarf, olive utility jacket and silver compact-camera strap

own.label: Ask about her motel photographs
own.player: Why photograph old motels?
own.reply: Because they’re where America keeps its secrets. Every motel sign is a promise someone broke.

own.label: Ask for a story
own.player: Tell me a Sunfall story.
own.reply: A woman ran the diner for forty years and never once took a day off. The day she died, the jukebox played her song by itself. Everyone swears it. I believe it.

own.label: Ask what her gala photo shows
own.player: What did you see in your gala photographs?
own.reply: A face at Table 9 who isn’t on the official guest list. Not a waiter, not a guest. Someone who wasn’t meant to be remembered.
own.note: Camille Baptiste photographed someone at Table 9 who isn’t on the official guest list.

own.label: Ask what photography taught her about people
own.player: What has photography taught you about people?
own.reply: That everyone has one honest face and they only show it when they think nobody’s looking. My job is to be nobody.

women.name: Tessa Larkin
women.look: Freckled fair skin, copper-red braids, bright coral top and faded jeans

own.label: Ask about the lizard
own.player: Did you get the lizard out of your kitchen?
own.reply: Eventually. His name is Gregory now. He lives in a shoebox and judges me.

own.label: Ask about her clay birds
own.player: You make clay birds?
own.reply: Terrible ones. They look like potatoes with opinions. I keep making them because I love birds and I’m not good at anything else, artistically.

own.label: Ask what she saw near the enclosure
own.player: Did you see something near the animal enclosure?
own.reply: A van with no plates parked by the bear trap the rangers didn’t set. Two men were checking a laptop. They drove off when I waved.
own.note: Tessa Larkin saw a van with no plates and two men with a laptop by an unofficial bear trap.

own.label: Ask what wild animals teach her
own.player: What do wild animals teach you?
own.reply: That you can’t love something into staying. You feed it, you heal it, and you open the box and let it go.

women.name: Nadia Okafor
women.look: Dark skin, shoulder-length box braids, burgundy shirt and simple watch

own.label: Ask about forensic work
own.player: Is forensic work like the TV shows?
own.reply: No. Less glowing blue lights, more labelling bags. But I love it. Details don’t lie. People do.

own.label: Ask about her crosswords
own.player: I hear you do cryptic crosswords?
own.reply: In diners, with a pencil, like a woman from a better century. A good clue is a crime scene: everything you need is there, disguised.

own.label: Ask what’s bothering her at work
own.player: Something at work bothering you?
own.reply: The chain-of-custody log for the gala evidence has a gap. Two hours where nobody signed for the bag. Nobody else seems to care.
own.note: Nadia Okafor found a two-hour gap in the custody log for the gala evidence.

own.label: Ask what evidence can’t prove
own.player: What can’t evidence prove?
own.reply: Why. I can tell you who was in a room and when. I can’t tell you why anyone does anything. That’s what keeps me up.

women.name: Marianne Keene
women.look: Dark skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, tortoiseshell glasses, emerald wrap dress

own.label: Ask about keeping the foundation’s books
own.player: What’s it like keeping the foundation’s books?
own.reply: Twenty years of other people’s generosity in my neat handwriting. I know who gives, who boasts and who quietly takes it back.

own.label: Ask about her souvenirs
own.player: I hear you collect roadside souvenirs?
own.reply: A plastic flamingo from a motel that’s now a car park, a spoon from the world’s second-largest cactus. Junk with a memory. Better than diamonds without one.

own.label: Ask what she overheard
own.player: You look like you overheard something you shouldn’t have.
own.reply: Two board members arguing in the cloakroom on gala night over a sealed envelope. One said, It burns tonight or we all do. I was holding someone’s mink at the time.
own.note: Marianne Keene overheard two board members on gala night arguing over a sealed envelope that had to burn tonight.

own.label: Ask what forty taught her
own.player: What has forty taught you?
own.reply: That you stop performing for people who aren’t watching. And that a good coat is worth any price.

women.name: Leona Carlisle
women.look: Fair skin, chestnut curly bob, grey-green eyes, navy shift dress with pearls

own.label: Ask what compliance actually means
own.player: What does a compliance administrator actually do?
own.reply: I make sure rich people fill in their forms correctly. They hate me in a very polite way. I’m invited to everything and spoken to by no one.

own.label: Ask about her watercolours
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: The desert, over and over. It’s the only thing in Sunfall that doesn’t want anything from me. I’m bad at it, which is the point.

own.label: Ask about the most impulsive thing she’s done
own.player: What’s the most impulsive thing you’ve ever done?
own.reply: I bought a horse at a charity auction because the bidding went quiet and I felt sorry for it. The horse and the auctioneer. I visit him whenever I need someone who won’t ask about my portfolio.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever broken a rule
own.player: Have you ever broken a rule yourself?
own.reply: Once. I signed off a form I knew was wrong because a frightened woman asked me to. Best thing I’ve done in that job. Worst thing for my career.

women.name: Elise Harrow
women.look: Warm brown skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, amber eyes, cream blazer over a silk camisole

own.label: Ask how she got the job
own.player: How did you end up keeping the foundation’s books?
own.reply: I was charming at the right party. Don’t look shocked. That’s how everyone here got their job; I’m just honest about it.

own.label: Ask about her singing
own.player: I heard you sing?
own.reply: In a little choir at St Brigid’s. I go for the music and stay because nobody there wants anything from me. Rare, in this town.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: Something’s bothering you. What is it?
own.reply: I have an invitation to a private dinner with my name on it. I don’t remember accepting it. Someone accepted it for me.
own.note: Elise Harrow has an invitation to a private dinner she never accepted.

own.label: Ask what she really wants
own.player: What do you really want, if you’re honest?
own.reply: To be someone people look at when I walk in. I know that’s shallow. Everyone wants it. I just say it out loud.

women.name: Francesca Quinn
women.look: Dark skin, brown waves with teal tips, a silver ear cuff, white linen trouser suit

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you actually do at the foundation?
own.reply: I make sure the rules are followed. Officially. Unofficially I make sure the right people know which rules exist.

own.label: Ask about her cookbooks
own.player: Someone said you collect cookbooks?
own.reply: Weird ones. A Victorian guide to dinner parties. A seventies one entirely about aspic. Every era thinks it has taste. Every era is wrong.

own.label: Ask what’s missing
own.player: Is something missing at work?
own.reply: One receipt. Gala night, a large cash withdrawal, signed off by someone who wasn’t there. I keep checking the drawer as if it’ll come back.
own.note: Francesca Quinn says a large cash withdrawal from gala night was signed off by someone who wasn’t there.

own.label: Ask what she cooks when she’s sad
own.player: What do you cook when you’re sad?
own.reply: My mother’s risotto. It takes forty minutes of stirring and you can’t leave it. It’s the only time I’m not thinking.

women.name: Naomi Whitlock
women.look: Medium-brown skin, natural afro puff, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, tailored grey waistcoat and slacks

own.label: Ask what a charity’s books reveal
own.player: What do you see, keeping a charity’s books?
own.reply: Every receipt tells a story. Most of them say lunch. A worrying number say lunch for twelve.

own.label: Ask about ballroom dancing
own.player: How’s the ballroom dancing going?
own.reply: My instructor says I lead with my head. I keep counting. Apparently you’re meant to feel it. I’ve never felt anything I didn’t first put in a spreadsheet.

own.label: Ask what it’s like being the youngest at the club
own.player: Is it strange being the youngest one at the club?
own.reply: Everyone calls me sweetheart and then asks me to fix their phone. I’ve set up the same woman’s email four times. She sends me fruit baskets.

own.label: Ask what she’s overthinking right now
own.player: What are you overthinking right now?
own.reply: Whether I replied too fast. Whether that sounded keen. Whether this sentence is too long. It is, isn’t it.

women.name: Bianca Roth
women.look: Olive skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, white linen trouser suit

own.label: Ask about her job at the foundation
own.player: What does a compliance administrator do all day?
own.reply: I make sure the right forms exist so that, if anyone ever asks, the right forms exist. It’s theatre, darling, with staples.

own.label: Ask about repairing watches
own.player: You repair watches?
own.reply: Old ones. Wind-up, no batteries, nothing that talks to your phone. A watch that keeps time without being told to is the most honest thing in this town.

own.label: Ask what she overheard
own.player: You look like you overheard something.
own.reply: Gala night, the back corridor: two board members arguing over a sealed envelope that had to be gone by morning. One of them saw me. Neither of them has looked at me since.
own.note: Bianca Roth heard two board members on gala night arguing over a sealed envelope that had to be gone by morning.

own.label: Ask why old watches matter to her
own.player: Why do old watches matter to you?
own.reply: Because someone made them to last a lifetime and they did. Name one thing you own that was built to outlive you.

women.name: Simone Ellery
women.look: Light-brown skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, a beauty mark above her lip, navy shift dress with pearls

women.name: Adeline Marsh
women.look: Tall and very slender, porcelain skin, a sharp aquiline nose, deep-set dark eyes with a cool sullen stare, a slim small-busted model figure, long red curls, a gold-buttoned navy blazer

women.name: Valerie Huxley
women.look: Rail-thin runway-model frame, a slim small-busted figure, translucent pale skin, high cheekbones, cool dark sullen eyes with faint shadows beneath, honey-blonde hair scraped back, a pale pink slip-style sheath dress

own.label: Ask about her balcony garden
own.player: What are you growing on that balcony?
own.reply: Basil, mint and a rosemary bush with ambitions. The mint is trying to take over. Honestly, I respect it.

own.label: Ask what she notices at the club
own.player: What do you notice that nobody else does at the club?
own.reply: Who pays, and who reaches for their wallet slowly. You could run the whole town’s gossip off that one detail.

own.label: Ask if numbers ever lie
own.player: Do numbers ever lie?
own.reply: Never. People lie with them all the time. I just put the numbers next to each other and wait.

own.label: Ask if she wants a different life
own.player: Do you ever want a completely different life?
own.reply: I want a small one. A kitchen with herbs on the sill and someone who comes home when he says he will. Everyone at the club wants more. I want enough.

women.name: Ruth Calder
women.look: Dark skin, short silver-dyed crop, rosy cheeks, powder-blue twinset

own.label: Ask about her twinsets
own.player: Do you really own that many twinsets?
own.reply: Eleven. In eleven shades of blue. My mother says a woman should always look as if she’s about to be photographed. Nobody has ever photographed me.

own.label: Ask about her pottery
own.player: How’s the pottery going?
own.reply: I made a vase for the club raffle and someone used it as an ashtray. I was so proud. It was being used.

own.label: Ask about her most awkward moment
own.player: What’s the most awkward thing you’ve ever done?
own.reply: I curtsied to the mayor. He’s a dentist. He was very kind about it, which made it worse.

own.label: Ask who her rival is
own.player: Is it true you have a rival at the club?
own.reply: Everyone has one. Mine wears red to annoy me. The terrible secret is that I like her, and I think she knows.

women.look: Deep brown skin, golden-brown ringlets, a silver ear cuff, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask about photographing crime scenes
own.player: What’s it like photographing crime scenes?
own.reply: You learn to look at the worst day of someone’s life as a problem of light. Then you go home and look at nothing for an hour.

own.label: Ask about the watches
own.player: You repair watches?
own.reply: Badly, slowly, happily. A watch is a crime scene in reverse: every part tells you exactly what happened, if you’re patient.

own.label: Ask what’s missing at work
own.player: Something missing at work?
own.reply: The key to the filing cabinet with the gala photographs. It was there, then it wasn’t, and the sign-out sheet is blank. Somebody in our own building wanted those prints.
own.note: Danica Holt says the key to the cabinet holding the gala crime-scene photographs went missing inside the police station.

own.label: Ask what colour she sees most at work
own.player: What colour do you see most at work?
own.reply: Beige. Carpets, walls, coats. The worst things happen in the most boring rooms.

women.name: Sasha Mahoney
women.look: Olive skin, natural afro puff, deep dimples, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask what the numbers say about Sunfall
own.player: What do the numbers say about Sunfall?
own.reply: Most accidents happen in the kitchen. Statistically, your toaster is a bigger threat than any stranger. Sleep well.

own.label: Ask about her book club
own.player: What’s your book club reading?
own.reply: Officially, a serious novel about grief. Actually, we drink wine and talk about our exes. Nobody has finished a book since we started.

own.label: Ask how a statistician can be impulsive
own.player: How is a statistician impulsive?
own.reply: I know the odds, so I ignore them. Knowing a thing is unlikely just makes me want to see it happen.

own.label: Ask which number she can’t forget
own.player: Is there a number you can’t forget?
own.reply: Seventeen. The number of calls a woman made before anyone came. I built a model so it would never happen again. It still happens.

women.name: Imani Harper
women.look: Pale skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, freckles across her nose, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask about the evidence archive
own.player: What’s the evidence archive like?
own.reply: Rows of boxes holding the worst days of people’s lives, sorted by number. I label them carefully. It feels like the least I can do.

own.label: Ask about her cactus garden
own.player: I heard you keep cacti indoors?
own.reply: Thirty-one of them. They’re the only things in Sunfall that thrive on neglect, and I respect that.

own.label: Ask what’s weighing on her
own.player: You seem like something’s weighing on you.
own.reply: I promised my mum I’d go home to Atlanta by now. I keep not going. Sunfall gets its hooks in you.

own.label: Ask about the box nobody opens
own.player: Is there a box in the archive nobody opens?
own.reply: Shelf nine, bottom row. It’s labelled with a case number that doesn’t exist. I’ve never opened it. I think about it every day.

women.name: Leila Sayeed
women.look: Olive skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, hazel eyes, plain white shirt and slim black trousers

own.label: Ask what a custody nurse does
own.player: What does a custody nurse actually do?
own.reply: I patch up people on the worst night of their lives, usually at both ends of the handcuffs. Everyone is polite to the nurse. Even the ones who bite.

own.label: Ask where she wants to be in ten years
own.player: Where do you want to be in ten years?
own.reply: Running the whole place. Or a little clinic by the sea. I change my mind every shift. Ambition is just restlessness with a plan.

own.label: Ask what she grows on her balcony
own.player: What are you growing out there?
own.reply: Mint for tea and chillies for revenge. Lavender too, for the nights I come home smelling of the station.

own.label: Ask what scares her at work
own.player: Does anything at work scare you?
own.reply: The quiet ones. The ones who say they’re fine and look at the wall. I’ve learned to sit with them a bit longer.

women.name: Joanne Kendrick
women.look: Freckled fair skin, natural afro puff, thin wire-rimmed glasses, maroon fleece and jeans

own.label: Ask what dispatch is like
own.player: What’s it like being a dispatcher?
own.reply: People ring me on the worst day of their lives and I have to sound calm. Then I hang up and shake. Then the next one rings.

own.label: Ask about her pottery
own.player: How’s the pottery going?
own.reply: I’ve made eleven bowls and none of them are round. My mum uses them anyway. She says they have character. They have holes.

own.label: Ask about the strangest call she’s taken
own.player: What’s the strangest call you’ve ever taken?
own.reply: A man who wanted us to arrest the moon because it was too bright. I logged it. Politely. You never know.

own.label: Ask how she switches off after a shift
own.player: How do you switch off after a shift?
own.reply: I don’t, really. I lie awake wondering how they all got on. You never find out. That’s the worst part.

women.name: Cassidy Boone
women.look: Fair skin, short silver-dyed crop, amber eyes, denim shirt with rolled sleeves

own.label: Ask what the records room is like
own.player: What’s it like down in the records room?
own.reply: Quiet. Dusty. Every file is somebody’s worst week, filed alphabetically. I like it down there. Paper doesn’t lie to you.

own.label: Ask about her sketches
own.player: What do you sketch?
own.reply: Old shopfronts before they’re knocked down. The barber’s, the cobbler’s, the old cinema. Somebody should remember what this town looked like.

own.label: Ask what loyalty means to her
own.player: What does loyalty mean to you?
own.reply: Turning up. Twice, if needed. Most people say they’d help you move house. I actually own a van.

own.label: Ask if a file ever stayed with her
own.player: Has a file ever stayed with you?
own.reply: One. An old case nobody closed. I read it every few weeks. Someone ought to keep looking, even if it’s only me.

women.name: Naoko Watanabe
women.look: Light-brown skin, blunt black bob, rosy cheeks, windbreaker over a sports top

women.name: Brenda Velasco
women.look: Lean and wiry, golden-tan skin, high sharp cheekbones, hooded dark eyes, a strong nose, a chestnut high ponytail, thin wire-rimmed glasses, an olive field jacket

own.label: Ask what a collision investigator does
own.player: What does a collision investigator actually do?
own.reply: I measure skid marks and work out who’s lying. Everyone says the other car came out of nowhere. Nothing comes out of nowhere.

own.label: Ask about her rescue dog
own.player: Tell me about your dog.
own.reply: Biscuit. He’s fourteen, half blind and convinced the postman is the devil. He sleeps on my feet. I’d die for him.

own.label: Ask what she’s most sceptical about
own.player: What are you most sceptical about?
own.reply: Men who say they’re great drivers. Every single one. I have the photographs.

own.label: Ask if the job changed how she drives
own.player: Has the job changed how you drive?
own.reply: I drive like my grandmother now. I hold my breath at every junction. I’ve seen what a second does.

women.name: Alisha Benton
women.look: Lean and athletic, olive skin, a slightly crooked nose from an old break, intense dark eyes, honey-blonde beach waves, a windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask if forensics is like on television
own.player: Is forensic work like it is on television?
own.reply: On television it takes an afternoon and a dramatic zoom. Here it takes a fortnight and a form. Nobody has ever said enhance to me.

own.label: Ask about her old cameras
own.player: What’s the appeal of old film cameras?
own.reply: You only get thirty-six chances, so you have to mean it. Phones turned everyone into people who take a thousand pictures of nothing.

own.label: Ask what she notices about people first
own.player: What do you notice about people first?
own.reply: Their hands. Bitten nails, paint, rings they keep turning. Hands tell you what faces are trained to hide.

own.label: Ask if there’s a film she’s never developed
own.player: Is there a roll of film you’ve never developed?
own.reply: One. My dad’s last roll. I’m scared it’s just the garden. I’m more scared it isn’t.

women.name: Adriana Ponce
women.look: Golden-tan skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, a beauty mark above her lip, overalls and a bandana

own.label: Ask why she campaigns
own.player: Why climate campaigning?
own.reply: Because my town in Sonora ran out of water when I was twelve. People argue about models. I remember the taps.

own.label: Ask about her football
own.player: Five-a-side, I heard?
own.reply: Every week with women half my age. I’m slower and dirtier. They’re learning a lot.

own.label: Ask what she makes of the young activists
own.player: What do you make of the younger activists?
own.reply: They’re brave and they’re online. They mistake a hashtag for a hard week’s work. I tell them: knock on doors, or go home. They hate me. They come back.

own.label: Ask what she got wrong when she was young
own.player: What did you get wrong when you were young?
own.reply: I thought shouting was the same as winning. It isn’t. The people I changed were the ones I had a coffee with.

women.name: Sienna Navarro
women.look: Olive skin, burgundy-dyed curls, grey-green eyes, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask what she’s organising
own.player: What are you organising at the moment?
own.reply: A mural on the underpass. Forty volunteers, three committees and one argument about whether a cactus is problematic. It’s a cactus.

own.label: Ask about the drums
own.player: How are the drums going?
own.reply: Loudly. My neighbour bangs on the wall in time now. I think we’re a band.

own.label: Ask what she overthinks most
own.player: What do you overthink the most?
own.reply: Group chats. If I put a full stop, am I angry? If I don’t, am I unserious? I once drafted a thumbs-up for ten minutes.

own.label: Ask if she ever tires of causes
own.player: Do you ever get tired of causes?
own.reply: All the time. Some days I just want to paint something pretty that doesn’t mean anything. I’m not allowed to say that at meetings.

women.name: Nora Hadley
women.look: Warm brown skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, a silver ear cuff, vintage windbreaker

own.label: Ask what her heresy is
own.player: What’s an opinion your friends hate?
own.reply: That nuclear power is the best thing for the climate. Say that in our group chat and watch people combust. Ironically.

own.label: Ask about learning Italian
own.player: You’re learning Italian?
own.reply: Badly. I want to read Dante in the original before I die. Ambitious, for someone who still says grazie wrong.

own.label: Ask what’s bothering her
own.player: Something on your mind?
own.reply: A woman from our march saw something on gala night. She told me, then a week later she told the police the exact opposite. Someone got to her.
own.note: Nora Hadley says a witness changed her story about gala night after someone got to her.

own.label: Ask what she believes that her friends don’t
own.player: What do you believe that your friends don’t?
own.reply: That men and women want different things, mostly, and that’s fine. Saying it at a meeting is like admitting you eat meat.

women.name: Daisy Chen
women.look: Dark skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, tortoiseshell glasses, hand-knitted jumper

own.label: Ask what she makes her collages from
own.player: What do you make the collages from?
own.reply: Old magazines, bus tickets, receipts people drop. I like turning things people threw away into something they’d stop to look at.

own.label: Ask why she’s bad at small talk
own.player: Why are you so bad at small talk?
own.reply: Because I’d rather know what you’re afraid of than what the weather is doing. It makes me very bad at parties and very good at funerals.

own.label: Ask about the worst crisis she’s handled
own.player: What’s the worst crisis you’ve handled?
own.reply: A pensioners’ craft fair where the glue gun caught fire. I put it out with a tea towel and nobody stopped knitting. Best day of my career.

own.label: Ask what she’s like when nobody’s watching
own.player: What are you like when nobody’s watching?
own.reply: Sillier. I dance in the kitchen and talk back to the radio. Most people only ever meet the organiser.

women.name: Zoe Whitaker
women.look: Light-brown skin, golden-brown ringlets, freckles across her nose, oversized thrifted cardigan

women.name: Khadija Rahman
women.look: Warm brown skin, cornrows into a low bun, strong dark brows, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask about her film nights
own.player: What do you show at the film nights?
own.reply: Old comedies, mostly. I tried a serious documentary once. Twelve people came and one of them was asleep. Now it’s slapstick and popcorn and the hall is full.

own.label: Ask what community meetings are really like
own.player: What are community meetings really like?
own.reply: Two hours, three people talking and a biscuit tin nobody opens until the end. The biscuits are the only thing everyone agrees on.

own.label: Ask what she disagrees with her friends about
own.player: What do you disagree with your friends about?
own.reply: Quite a lot, quietly. They think everything is a system. I think a lot of things are just people being rude. You can’t fix rude with a workshop.

own.label: Ask what she misses most
own.player: What do you miss most?
own.reply: My grandmother’s kitchen. Everyone shouting and nobody angry. Sunfall is very polite. I miss being shouted at with love.

women.name: Esther Yu
women.look: Medium-brown skin, glossy black ponytail, a silver ear cuff, oversized thrifted cardigan

women.name: Cassandra Finch
women.look: Bird-like and slight, warm brown skin, cropped bleached hair, enormous dark tired eyes with a sullen look, a small gap between her front teeth, a slim small-busted figure, a linen shirt and a canvas tote

own.label: Ask how she stays so cheerful
own.player: How do you stay so cheerful?
own.reply: Stubbornness. I decided to be cheerful years ago and I refuse to back down now. Out of spite, mainly.

own.label: Ask what she paints
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: Skies. Sunfall has the best skies in the world and everyone is looking at their phones under them. Sorry. Not you. Well, a bit you.

own.label: Ask if she fits in with her group
own.player: Do you fit in with the others?
own.reply: Not really. I go to the meetings, bring the cake and vote how I like. They keep me for the cake.

own.label: Ask what she’ll never give up on
own.player: What will you never give up on?
own.reply: People. Even the awful ones. Especially the awful ones. Someone gave up on me once, and it took years to undo.

women.name: Eden Sutherland
women.look: Waifish and slight, a slim small-busted figure, light-brown skin, freckles across her nose, huge dark sleepy eyes with a sullen stare, buzz-cut dark hair, a gap-toothed smile, overalls and a bandana

own.label: Ask what campaigning is like day to day
own.player: What’s campaigning actually like day to day?
own.reply: Leaflets, rain and men in big cars telling me to get a job. This is my job. It pays less than their car.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: Alto. Church hall, old ladies, hymns I don’t believe in. It’s the only place I feel calm. Don’t tell my friends.

own.label: Ask why she’s so blunt
own.player: Why are you so blunt?
own.reply: Because the world’s on fire and I haven’t got time to be nice about it. I’m nice afterwards. I bring soup.

own.label: Ask what she gives away
own.player: What do you give away?
own.reply: Most of my wages, honestly. My flatmate calls it a problem. I call it the only bit of my life that makes sense.

women.name: Agnes Castillo
women.look: Deep brown skin, box braids to the waist, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, soft cream jumper and long pleated skirt

own.label: Ask about the parish garden
own.player: What grows in a desert parish garden?
own.reply: Roses, if you’re stubborn. Prickly pear, if you’re sensible. We grow both, which is very Catholic of us.

own.label: Ask about the ballroom dancing
own.player: You’re learning ballroom dancing?
own.reply: Yes, and I’m dreadful. It’s good for me. You have to let someone else lead, which I find very hard.

own.label: Ask what she’s worried about
own.player: You seem worried about something.
own.reply: There’s a payment in the parish books to a company I’ve never heard of. Nobody will explain it. I’ve prayed about it and I still want an answer.
own.note: Agnes Castillo found an unexplained parish payment to an unknown company.

own.label: Ask what grows best in the desert
own.player: What grows best in the desert?
own.reply: Things that wait. Seeds sit for years until the rain comes. My grandmother called it faith with roots.

women.name: Eliza Montoya
women.look: Warm brown skin, box braids to the waist, freckles across her nose, soft cream jumper and long pleated skirt

own.label: Ask about the food pantry
own.player: What’s the food pantry like?
own.reply: Busy and quiet at the same time. People come in ashamed and leave a little less ashamed. That’s the real work. The tins are just the excuse.

own.label: Ask why she volunteers
own.player: Why do you give so much of your time?
own.reply: Because it was given to me first. When my family had nothing, the Sisters fed us and never once made us feel small. I owe them the rest of my life, gladly.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: You seem troubled.
own.reply: The pantry’s storeroom has a filing cabinet nobody uses, and now it’s locked and the key is gone. Someone is keeping something in a place nobody thinks to look.
own.note: Eliza Montoya says an unused filing cabinet in the food pantry’s storeroom is now locked and its key is missing.

own.label: Ask who comes to the pantry
own.player: Who comes to the food pantry?
own.reply: People you’d never guess. A nurse. A man in a suit who cried. Pride is the hardest thing anyone carries through that door.

women.name: Rosalie Kemp
women.look: Pale skin, sandy shag with a fringe, a beauty mark above her lip, long-sleeved maxi dress

own.label: Ask about the chapel archive
own.player: What’s in the chapel archive?
own.reply: Baptisms, marriages and funerals back to when Sunfall was a mission. Every name in this town is in my books somewhere.

own.label: Ask about her book club
own.player: You run a book club?
own.reply: Six women, one bottle of sherry and a lot of arguing about Jane Austen. It’s the most honest room in the parish.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: Something’s troubling you.
own.reply: Our caretaker vanished without collecting his wages. A man who never missed Mass. He looked after the bell tower.
own.note: Rosalie Kemp says the chapel caretaker, who looked after the bell tower, vanished without collecting his wages.

own.label: Ask what the old records say about love
own.player: What do the old parish records say about love?
own.reply: Marriages that lasted sixty years, recorded in two lines. No photographs, no speeches. Just two names and a lifetime.

women.name: Bernadette Flores
women.look: Rosy fair skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, sage cardigan and long linen skirt

own.label: Ask about conserving old things
own.player: What does a conservator actually do?
own.reply: I keep beautiful things from falling apart a little longer. Paintings, vestments, people, occasionally.

own.label: Ask why new things look so cheap
own.player: Why does everything new look so cheap?
own.reply: Because we stopped making things to last. Our grandparents built for their grandchildren. We build for the next quarterly report.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: I promised my father I’d marry in the chapel where he married my mother. I nearly gave up on that promise. I’ve started believing in it again.

own.label: Ask why she repairs instead of replaces
own.player: Why repair things instead of replacing them?
own.reply: Because a mended thing has a story. A new thing just has a price. We throw away so much now, people included.

women.name: Lucia Romano
women.look: Deep brown skin, long locs with gold cuffs, strong dark brows, blouse with a Peter Pan collar

women.name: Odette Price
women.look: Olive skin, black space buns, amber eyes, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask about local radio
own.player: What’s it like working in local radio?
own.reply: Lovely and doomed. The phone-in callers are the loneliest people in town, and they’re the best part of the show.

own.label: Ask about her sketches
own.player: You sketch old shopfronts?
own.reply: Before they’re turned into vape shops. I’ve drawn eleven that are gone now. It’s a sort of memorial.

own.label: Ask about the letter
own.player: Is something worrying you?
own.reply: An unsigned letter came to my flat. It said stop asking about the junction. I hadn’t asked about the junction yet.
own.note: Odette Price got an unsigned letter telling her to stop asking about the junction.

own.label: Ask whose voice she misses
own.player: Is there a voice you miss?
own.reply: My grandfather read the shipping forecast on local radio for thirty years. Nobody needed it in the desert. He read it anyway, like a prayer.

women.name: Arielle Brooks
women.look: Golden-tan skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, freckles across her nose, bomber jacket and graphic tee

own.label: Ask about the newspaper archive
own.player: What do you find in the Sunfall Daily archive?
own.reply: A hundred years of the town lying to itself in very nice fonts. My favourite headline is from the drought years: Rain Expected Any Day Now. It wasn’t.

own.label: Ask about stargazing
own.player: You go stargazing in the desert?
own.reply: Every clear night. Out past the canyon the sky is so full it’s almost loud. You remember how small Sunfall is, and how small its scandals are.

own.label: Ask about the favour
own.player: Has someone asked you for a favour?
own.reply: An old friend wants me to lose a box of clippings about the old chapel’s last caretaker. She’s never asked me for anything before. That’s what worries me.
own.note: Arielle Brooks was asked by an old friend to lose archive clippings about the old chapel’s last caretaker.

own.label: Ask which star she’d name after you
own.player: If you named a star after me, which one?
own.reply: A dim one. Don’t be offended. The dim ones are the ones you only find if you’re really looking.

women.name: Harper Lin
women.look: Freckled fair skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, deep dimples, striped shirt and trench coat

own.label: Ask what goes into the weekend paper
own.player: What goes into the weekend paper?
own.reply: Recipes, the crossword and one serious story I fight for every single week. People only read the crossword, so I put the serious story next to it.

own.label: Ask about her old dog
own.player: Tell me about your dog.
own.reply: Pickle. Thirteen, deaf as a post, and asleep under my desk at the paper. She’s our longest-serving member of staff.

own.label: Ask about her favourite headline
own.player: What’s your favourite headline you ever wrote?
own.reply: GOAT EATS MAYOR’S SPEECH. True story. It was a very good speech, apparently. The goat agreed.

own.label: Ask about a story she never ran
own.player: Is there a story you never ran?
own.reply: One. The facts were right and it would have ruined a good woman for one bad week. I spiked it. I still don’t know if that was journalism or cowardice.

women.name: Delia Maher
women.look: Pale skin, twist-out coils, deep dimples, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask how she got so far so young
own.player: You’re young for an investigative reporter.
own.reply: I’m patient for a young person. That’s the trick. Everyone else my age wants to go viral. I want to be right.

own.label: Ask about her old cameras
own.player: You restore old film cameras?
own.reply: Film makes you think before you shoot. Digital lets you shoot instead of thinking. Same with opinions.

own.label: Ask about the ruined recording
own.player: What’s on the recording you’re restoring?
own.reply: A voicemail from the night of the gala. Half of it is static. The other half is a woman saying not Table 9, the kitchen.
own.note: Delia Maher is restoring a gala-night voicemail: a woman says not Table 9, the kitchen.

own.label: Ask if she ever feels too young for her job
own.player: Do you ever feel too young for your job?
own.reply: Every press conference. Old men call me sweetheart, and then they read what I wrote about them. Nobody calls me sweetheart twice.

women.name: Zadie Foster
women.look: Light-brown skin, ash-blonde lob, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, utility vest with many pockets

own.label: Ask about reviewing music
own.player: What’s reviewing music like?
own.reply: Free tickets and a lot of enemies. Bands remember a bad review forever. One drummer still sends me a postcard every year that just says no.

own.label: Ask if she’s any good at pool
own.player: Are you any good at pool?
own.reply: Dangerously. My neighbours play for washing-up duty. I haven’t washed a plate in two years.

own.label: Ask about the best gig she’s seen
own.player: What’s the best gig you’ve ever seen?
own.reply: A girl with a broken guitar in the back room of the Lucky Cactus. Eleven people. She played like there were thousands. I gave her five stars and she cried.

own.label: Ask if she’d ever stop writing
own.player: Would you ever stop writing?
own.reply: Every rejection makes me want to. Then I hear a song I need to tell someone about, and I’m back. It’s less a job than an affliction.

women.name: Celina Rojas
women.look: Warm beige skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, rosy cheeks, press lanyard and denim jacket

own.label: Ask what a photography assistant does
own.player: What does a photography assistant actually do?
own.reply: Carry everything, hold the reflector and get blamed for the weather. One day I’ll take the picture. Today I hold the bag.

own.label: Ask about the bicycle
own.player: How’s the bike coming along?
own.reply: It has two wheels now. Neither of them goes round. I’ve watched forty videos about chains and I understand less than when I started.

own.label: Ask about the best picture she’s helped take
own.player: What’s the best picture you’ve helped take?
own.reply: An old cowboy at the rodeo, laughing with no teeth. My boss got the credit. I got the cowboy’s number. He rings me on my birthday.

own.label: Ask what keeps her up at night
own.player: What keeps you up at night?
own.reply: Whether I’m good enough or just keen. Whether keen runs out. Whether you can tell I reread my messages six times before I send them.

women.name: Kira Henson
women.look: Warm beige skin, burgundy-dyed curls, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, cable-knit jumper and leather satchel

own.label: Ask what court reporting is like
own.player: What’s court reporting like?
own.reply: I sit in the same room as the worst things people do and write down every word. You learn to hear what people don’t say. The pauses are where the truth is.

own.label: Ask where her hidden routes go
own.player: Where do your hidden hiking routes go?
own.reply: Old mining paths, dry riverbeds, a cave nobody marks on the map. I draw them by hand, and I only share them with people I trust.

own.label: Ask about her oldest friend
own.player: Who’s your oldest friend?
own.reply: A girl from my first newsroom. We fell out for six years over nothing. Then her dad died and I was on her doorstep within the hour. That’s friendship. Turning up.

own.label: Ask if a verdict ever felt wrong
own.player: Has a verdict ever felt wrong to you?
own.reply: Once. I wrote it up straight, the way you have to. Then I walked into the desert and stayed until dark. The desert doesn’t argue.

women.name: Moira Bell
women.look: Waifish and very pale, a slim small-busted model figure, faint shadows under dark sullen eyes, bleached eyebrows, golden-brown ringlets, a small nose stud, a striped shirt under an oversized trench coat

own.label: Ask what a fact-checker does
own.player: What does a fact-checker actually do?
own.reply: I ring people and ask if they really said what they said. Most of them didn’t. I remember everything anyone tells me. It’s a gift, mostly.

own.label: Ask about teaching her cousin guitar
own.player: How are the guitar lessons going?
own.reply: He’s eleven and only wants to learn one song. I’ve taught it to him eighty times. I don’t mind. I like it when people need me.

own.label: Ask why she hates small talk
own.player: Why do you hate small talk?
own.reply: Because it’s a waste of a person. I’d rather know one true thing about you than a hundred nice ones. Tell me one true thing.

own.label: Ask what she remembers about you
own.player: What do you remember about me so far?
own.reply: Everything. What you said first, what you didn’t answer, how long you took to reply. Sorry. That came out intense. It’s the job.

women.name: Talia Farouk
women.look: Light olive skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, tortoiseshell glasses, rolled-sleeve oxford shirt

own.label: Ask about her travel column
own.player: What do you write about in your travel column?
own.reply: Places nobody visits on purpose. A motel with one working sign, a diner with the best pie for two hundred miles. Readers send me hate mail and then go there.

own.label: Ask about her forgotten records
own.player: What kind of records do you collect?
own.reply: Ones nobody else remembers. Singers who made one album and vanished. I like to think somebody somewhere is still singing in the shower, unaware they’re a cult classic.

own.label: Ask what she’s sceptical of
own.player: What are you sceptical of?
own.reply: Hidden gems. Every hidden gem has a gift shop now. The real ones don’t know they’re hidden.

own.label: Ask where she feels at home
own.player: Where do you feel most at home?
own.reply: On a bus at night, with nowhere to be for six hours. Everyone else calls it travel. I call it the only time my head is quiet.

women.name: Sable Marlow
women.look: Light olive skin, dark French braid, a beauty mark above her lip, black lace corset top

own.label: Ask about running a music venue
own.player: What’s it like running a venue?
own.reply: Glamorous for ten minutes a night. The rest is mopping and arguing with drummers.

own.label: Ask about her football
own.player: You play five-a-side?
own.reply: Goalkeeper. I like standing in the way of things. Ask my exes.

own.label: Ask about the borrowed camera
own.player: Why did you borrow someone’s camera?
own.reply: The house photographer left it behind after the last goth night. One photo’s been deleted. Who deletes one photo? Someone with something in it.
own.note: A camera left at Sable Marlow’s venue after goth night has one deleted photo.

own.label: Ask about the best night at her venue
own.player: What was the best night your venue ever had?
own.reply: A band nobody had heard of played to forty people in a storm. The power cut, and they kept going acoustic. Nobody went home.

women.name: Lenore Vale
women.look: Golden-tan skin, sandy shag with a fringe, strong dark brows, studded leather jacket

own.label: Ask if she’s related to Professor Vale
own.player: Any relation to Professor Vale?
own.reply: None. Probably. My grandmother would have said every Vale is cousin to a scandal.

own.label: Ask about her jewellery
own.player: What do you make?
own.reply: Silver mourning jewellery. Lockets for hair, rings for the dead. People think it’s morbid. I think it’s love that refuses to stop.

own.label: Ask about her strangest order
own.player: What’s the strangest order you’ve had?
own.reply: Thirteen crescent pendants, paid in cash, collected by a girl who wouldn’t take her sunglasses off. I make a mark on everything I cast. I’d know them anywhere.
own.note: Lenore Vale cast thirteen crescent pendants for a cash order, and marks everything she makes.

own.label: Ask what she’d make for someone she loved
own.player: What would you make for someone you loved?
own.reply: A ring that doesn’t look like a ring. Something only the two of us would know meant anything.

women.name: Ashlyn Vex
women.look: Dark skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, a small nose stud, velvet choker and black slip dress

own.label: Ask about running the venue
own.player: What’s it like running a music venue?
own.reply: Mopping beer off the floor at the end of the night while a band argues about their fee. I wouldn’t swap it for anything. The floor is sticky with history.

own.label: Ask why she’s learning Italian
own.player: Why are you learning Italian?
own.reply: So I can be dramatic in a language that deserves it. English doesn’t have enough words for despair. Italian has a whole opera.

own.label: Ask about the worst band she’s booked
own.player: Who’s the worst band you’ve ever booked?
own.reply: A trio who played one note, very slowly, for an hour. They called it a protest. Against what, nobody found out. They sold out.

own.label: Ask what she’s restless for
own.player: What are you restless for?
own.reply: Somewhere that isn’t here. Then I get there and miss the sticky floor. I think home is just the place you complain about most.

women.name: Morrigan Hale
women.look: Fair skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, tortoiseshell glasses, black lace corset top

own.label: Ask about her jewellery
own.player: What kind of jewellery do you make?
own.reply: Silver bats, tiny coffins, rings shaped like thorns. Brides buy them for their bridesmaids now. Goth has gone mainstream, and I’ve never been richer or sadder.

own.label: Ask about her collages
own.player: What do you make collages from?
own.reply: Old funeral cards and pressed flowers. It sounds morbid. It’s the most hopeful thing I do. Everyone in them was loved by someone.

own.label: Ask if she really breaks hearts
own.player: Is it true you break hearts?
own.reply: I don’t break them. I just leave before they get attached, and that hurts more than breaking. I’m working on staying. Slowly.

own.label: Ask what would make her stay
own.player: What would make you stay?
own.reply: Someone who notices when I go quiet and doesn’t panic. Someone who makes tea and waits. That’s all. Nobody waits.

women.name: Cleo Rook
women.look: Pale skin, box braids to the waist, sharp winged eyeliner, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask about her venue
own.player: What’s your venue like?
own.reply: An old converted church with bad acoustics and a good bar. I’ve run it for twelve years. The bands get younger. The ghosts stay the same.

own.label: Ask about her travel journal
own.player: Where has your travel journal been?
own.reply: Lisbon, Prague, a bus station in the middle of nowhere for nine hours. I write by hand, because a phone forgets and paper doesn’t.

own.label: Ask what she’s proudest of
own.player: What are you proudest of?
own.reply: Never selling the venue to the people who wanted to turn it into flats. They offered a lot. I told them it was haunted. It is.

own.label: Ask about the ghost
own.player: Is your venue really haunted?
own.reply: Something hums in the old vestry when the room is empty. I leave the light on for it. Everyone deserves someone who leaves a light on.

women.name: Veda Thorn
women.look: Dark skin, honey-blonde beach waves, freckles across her nose, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask how she makes her jewellery
own.player: How do you make your pieces?
own.reply: Lost-wax casting, a gas torch and swearing. The swearing is what gives them character.

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: What do you show at your film night?
own.reply: Old horror films in a back room with a bedsheet for a screen. The jumps are better when the projector jumps too.

own.label: Ask why she skips small talk
own.player: Why do you skip the small talk?
own.reply: Because I’d rather argue with you about whether vampires are romantic. They’re not. They’re landlords.

own.label: Ask how she stays calm in a crisis
own.player: How do you stay so calm in a crisis?
own.reply: I fall apart beforehand, in private, in great detail. When the crisis comes I’m all used up. Calm is just exhaustion with good posture.

women.name: Nixie Adler
women.look: Freckled fair skin, dark French braid, thin wire-rimmed glasses, plum corset dress

own.label: Ask about her roadside souvenirs
own.player: What’s in your souvenir collection?
own.reply: A snow globe of a petrol station, a plastic alien from a diner and a spoon from a town with a population of nine. I love things nobody else would keep.

own.label: Ask what running the venue taught her
own.player: What has running the venue taught you?
own.reply: That the quiet kid at the back will be famous in five years, and the loud one will owe me money. Every time.

own.label: Ask what she’s sceptical of
own.player: What are you sceptical of?
own.reply: Anyone who says they’re an old soul. Babe, you’re twenty-two. I have socks older than your soul.

own.label: Ask who looked after her when she was young
own.player: Who looked after you when you were young?
own.reply: A woman who ran a record shop and let me sit there all day when home was bad. I run the venue for kids like me. Somebody has to leave the door open.

women.name: Lavinia Gravesend
women.look: Thin and very pale, a long narrow face with hollow cheeks, kohl-smudged dark sullen eyes, a slim small-busted figure, a glossy black ponytail, a black mesh top and a tartan skirt

own.label: Ask about her jewellery
own.player: What do you make?
own.reply: Lockets, mostly. People put photographs and locks of hair in them, the way people did a hundred and fifty years ago. It sounds creepy. It’s the most romantic thing in the world.

own.label: Ask about her watercolours
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: The desert in the evening, very badly. I paint everything purple. My tutor said that’s not how colour works. I said that’s how it works for me.

own.label: Ask what she’s noticed about you
own.player: What have you noticed about me?
own.reply: You ask questions and then actually wait for the answer. That’s rarer than you’d think. Most men are just reloading.

own.label: Ask what she’d put in her own locket
own.player: What would you put in your own locket?
own.reply: Nothing yet. I keep it empty on purpose. It feels like a promise I haven’t made to anyone.

women.name: Raven Solis
women.look: Pale skin, platinum pixie cut, strong dark brows, black mesh top and tartan skirt

own.label: Ask what it’s like running a venue so young
own.player: What’s it like running a venue at your age?
own.reply: Bands think I’m the merch girl until I tell them their fee. Then they think I’m terrifying. Both are true.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: I sing hymns in black lipstick. The old ladies were scared of me for a month. Now they knit me scarves. Black ones, specially.

own.label: Ask why she’s so mysterious
own.player: Why are you so mysterious?
own.reply: I’m not. I just don’t know what to say most of the time, so I say nothing, and people decide it means something.

own.label: Ask what she’d sing if nobody was listening
own.player: What would you sing if nobody was listening?
own.reply: Something cheerful. A really stupid pop song. Don’t tell anyone. It would ruin the whole thing I’ve got going.

women.name: Kayla Mendoza
women.look: Dark skin, blunt black bob, grey-green eyes, floral blouse and jeans

own.label: Ask about decorating people’s homes
own.player: What’s it like decorating people’s homes?
own.reply: Everyone wants a calm neutral palette and then cries when they see it. I tell them grey is a mood, not a personality.

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: What do you show at your film night?
own.reply: Romcoms, unapologetically. The neighbours bring wine and shout at the screen when he runs to the airport. We know he’ll make it. We need him to.

own.label: Ask about her worst impulse buy
own.player: What’s your worst impulse buy?
own.reply: A velvet sofa the colour of a flamingo. It doesn’t fit through my door. It lives in my sister’s garage. I visit it.

own.label: Ask what her own home is like
own.player: What’s your own home like?
own.reply: Unfinished. I do everyone else’s and never mine. I think I’m waiting until there’s someone to choose the curtains with.

women.name: Brittany Hale
women.look: Light-brown skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, sharp winged eyeliner, turquoise peasant top

own.label: Ask about her souvenirs
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Roadside souvenirs! A snow globe of a cactus, a spoon from a motel that burned down, a fridge magnet of the bear. I need help.

own.label: Ask about being a florist
own.player: What’s the best part of being a florist?
own.reply: Weddings. The worst part is weddings. Brides cry, mothers cry, I cry, the flowers wilt.

own.label: Ask what’s confusing her
own.player: Is something confusing you?
own.reply: Two people told me completely different stories about the same night of the gala. One of them is lying, and they both bought peonies.

own.label: Ask what flowers say that people can’t
own.player: What do flowers say that people can’t?
own.reply: Sorry, mostly. I sell more sorry than love. Men walk in looking at the floor and point at the roses.

women.name: Nina Petrov
women.look: Rosy fair skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, thin wire-rimmed glasses, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask about her bakery
own.player: How did a pastry chef end up in the desert?
own.reply: I followed a man here from St Petersburg. The man left. The ovens stayed. I chose the ovens.

own.label: Ask about her painting
own.player: You paint watercolours?
own.reply: Desert landscapes. Watercolour is like this town: you can’t correct a mistake, only paint over it and hope.

own.label: Ask about the torn page
own.player: Why do you keep a torn notebook?
own.reply: A customer left a notebook at the counter with one page torn out. The next page shows the impression of the writing: a list of table numbers and a time I can’t read.
own.note: Nina Petrov has a notebook left at her counter; the page after a torn-out one shows an impression of table numbers.

own.label: Ask what she’d do over
own.player: If you could do one thing over, what would it be?
own.reply: I’d have said yes to a man who asked me to dance at a wedding in my twenties. I said I was tired. I wasn’t tired.

women.name: Jessica Rivera
women.look: Olive skin, rose-gold bob, a beauty mark above her lip, striped T-shirt dress

own.label: Ask what the pharmacy is like
own.player: What’s it like working in a pharmacy?
own.reply: People tell me things they wouldn’t tell their doctor while I find their ointment. I know half of Sunfall’s secrets and all of its rashes.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: Second soprano, hidden at the back. I mouth the high notes. Nobody has noticed in four years, or they’re too polite to say.

own.label: Ask if she’s shy or just careful
own.player: Are you shy, or just careful?
own.reply: Both. I rehearse phone calls in the shower. I once said you too to a waiter who told me to enjoy my meal. I still think about it.

own.label: Ask what she’d do if she weren’t scared
own.player: What would you do if you weren’t scared?
own.reply: Sing a solo. Just once. Loud, at the front, with everyone looking. Then probably faint.

women.name: Alana Brooks
women.look: Deep brown skin, honey-blonde beach waves, a silver ear cuff, mint polo shirt

own.label: Ask about the museum
own.player: What’s it like working at the museum?
own.reply: Quiet, cool and full of things people loved enough to keep. I tell school groups not to touch, and then I let the shy kids touch one thing.

own.label: Ask about her cookbooks
own.player: I hear you collect strange cookbooks?
own.reply: A church fundraiser book from the fifties with eleven recipes for jelly salad. Every family in it is listed by name. It’s the best history of Sunfall I own.

own.label: Ask what’s worrying her
own.player: Something on your mind?
own.reply: A woman who used to clean at the museum saw something on the gala night and told me. Now she tells everyone she was home all night. People don’t forget like that. They get frightened like that.
own.note: Alana Brooks says a museum cleaner who saw something on gala night now claims she was home all night.

own.label: Ask what she’d put in a museum of her life
own.player: What would go in a museum of your life?
own.reply: A burnt pan, a library card, and a letter I never sent. The letter would be the main exhibit.

women.name: Samantha Price
women.look: Warm beige skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, mint polo shirt

women.name: Jade Carter
women.look: Waifish and slight, a slim small-busted figure, pale freckled skin, wide-set grey eyes with a sleepy sullen gaze, a gap-toothed smile, golden-brown ringlets, an oversized yellow sundress

women.name: Karina Flores
women.look: Slight and narrow-shouldered, pale freckled skin, wide-set heavy-lidded eyes, a strong nose, an ash-blonde lob, a sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask what tourists ask her
own.player: What do tourists ask you?
own.reply: Whether the cacti are real, whether the desert is always this hot and whether I’m single. Yes, yes, and it depends on the tip.

own.label: Ask what her book club reads
own.player: What does your book club read?
own.reply: Thrillers where the husband did it. Every time. We’re a very suspicious book club. Two members have since divorced.

own.label: Ask about Sunfall’s best-kept secret
own.player: What’s Sunfall’s best-kept secret?
own.reply: A hot spring past the old drive-in, behind a fence that says no entry. Nobody checks. I only take people there off the books.

own.label: Ask if she’d ever leave Sunfall
own.player: Would you ever leave Sunfall?
own.reply: I show people this town every day, so I know how small it is. Still, I keep finding new corners. Maybe I’m waiting for a reason to stay.
